library(kableExtra)
library(dplyr)

# Methods {#sec:methods}

We conducted a study involving K–12 students from two schools to investigate how interactions with AI agents influence students’ self-confidence and task performance, as well as their perceptions of the helpfulness of AI assistance across different tasks. Students interacted with a custom-designed web application, the "AI Agent", which randomly assigned them to distinct conditions during structured educational activities. The study featured two manipulations, which we describe in detail below. To evaluate their effects, we collected objective measures of task performance and administered pre- and post-task questions to capture students' cognitive and affective responses. The following subsections describe the experimental procedures, the design of the AI agent, and the participants' characteristics.

## Experimental Manipulations

Figure \@ref(fig:manipulations) illustrates the two experimental manipulations: (1) AI advice with vs without explanation and (2) Socratic vs non-Socratic AI agents. Each manipulation consists of two conditions. Students were randomly assigned to one condition within each manipulation, with the two assignments conducted independently. Given the independent randomisation procedures, assignment to one manipulation does not systematically influence the estimated treatment effect of the other, although it may contribute to greater estimate uncertainty.

```{r manipulations, fig.cap = cap}
cap <- paste(
  "The study involves two randomised manipulations:",
  "**A.** Socratic vs Non-Socratic AI agents;",
  "**B.** AI advice with explanation vs AI advice without explanation"
)
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("assets/pictures/experimental_design.pdf"))
```

### Manipulation 1: AI Advice With vs Without Explanation

Students were first asked to independently guess the total value of the coins in a jar, without AI assistance (see Section \@ref(sec:si-ai-explanation) for the details).[^jar] They were then shown advice from the AI Agent and asked to revise their initial guess based on that advice.

We adapted the coin-jar task from Steiner's experiment, originally designed to assess the guessing accuracy of Internet users [@steiner2015turns]. We manipulated the level of detail in the AI Agent's advice across two conditions. In both conditions, the AI provided the same estimated value ($213). However, in the explanation condition, the AI presented its estimate alongside a step-by-step explanation of how it derived the estimate from the jar image.[^jar-gpt4] In the prediction-only condition, the AI provided the same estimate without any accompanying explanation.

[^jar]: This is a common experimental activity in economics, especially in the context of auction theory [@thaler1988anomalies]. The task is ideal in our setting because it requires participants to guess based on limited information, thus creating a situation where AI-generated assistance could potentially influence their decisions.

[^jar-gpt4]: Using GPT 4.0, we uploaded the image of the coin jar asking for an estimate of the value of coins ten times. We then selected the median response for the experiment.

This setup allows us to examine how complementing AI assistance with step-by-step explanation may affect students' performance and their perceptions of the AI's accuracy. Specifically, we focus on three outcome variables: (1) the propensity to update and direction of the update relative to their initial guess; (2) the accuracy of students' final estimations, measured as the (absolute) difference between their final guesses and the actual coin value; and (3) students' perceived accuracy of the AI advice, rated on a five-point scale from low to high. We also asked participants (4) to rate the perceived accuracy of the mean guess among 600 people ($596), which exaggerated the correct value, as reported in the original article [@steiner2015turns].

### Manipulation 2: Socratic vs Non-Socratic AI Agents

Next, students were asked to complete a series of three tasks, for which they could use an AI agent for assistance. The second manipulation involved randomly assigning students to one of two types of AI agents: Socratic or non-Socratic. Although both agents were powered by the same underlying large language model (GPT-4), they were instructed to behave differently through distinct system messages, as illustrated in Table \@ref(tab:prompts). Specifically, the Socratic agent was instructed to engage students through open-ended, thought-provoking questions that encouraged critical thinking and reflection on their responses. In contrast, the non-Socratic agent was instructed to provide concise, direct answers, without necessarily encouraging deeper dialogue or asking follow-up questions.

```{r prompts}
socratic_prompt <- paste(
  "You are a Socratic tutor.",
  "You always answer using the Socratic style, asking just the right questions to help students learn to think for themselves and breaking down the problem into simpler parts until it's at the right level for them. You provide concise information and explanations understandable for 8th to 10th grade students." # nolint
)
didactic_prompt <- paste(
  "You are a didactic tutor.",
  "You provide concise information and explanations understandable for 8th to 10th grade students." # nolint
)

data.frame(
  "AI Agent" = c("Socratic", "Non Socratic"),
  "Prompt instruction" = c(socratic_prompt, didactic_prompt),
  check.names = FALSE
) %>%
  kableExtra::kbl(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    linesep = c("\\addlinespace"),
    caption = "Prompt instructions associated with the AI-Agent conditions"
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, "4in")
```

This setup allows us to investigate the impact of different pedagogical AI tutoring approaches on students' performance and perceptions. Specifically, we asked students to use the AI Agent while performing three tasks: guess an unknown quantity ("How much water in litres do students consume at our school each week?"), express an opinion and write a short essay ("What is your opinion about the effect of social media on teenagers?"); respond to physics questions on how sound propagates in different media ("In which of the following materials does sound travel faster?"). These questions enabled us to assess the AI agent's impact on students' learning and problem-solving abilities. 

We focused on two primary metrics: (1) confidence in their answers and (2) perceived usefulness of interacting with the AI agent. Specifically,  students were asked, "How confident are you that the answer you provided is accurate?" on a five-point scale ranging from "not confident at all" to "very confident." They were also asked, "How helpful was it to interact with the AI tutor?" This was also rated on a five-point scale, from "Not at all helpful" to "Very helpful." Only for task 3, we had an additional metric, which was the correctness of their answers.

## Participants

We recruited students between 14 and 16 years old enrolled in secondary education from two schools. Both schools are bilingual secondary institutions that follow a European curriculum framework, with English as the primary language of instruction across most subjects. One school was in Brussels, Belgium, and the other in Seville, Spain. The choice of recruiting schools from different countries was to increase the external validity of our study.^[
    The country choice was by convenience as the authors lived in Brussels and Seville at the time of the experiment.
]

The student populations at both schools are culturally and linguistically diverse, including a mix of local and expatriate families. Many students come from middle- to upper-middle-class socioeconomic backgrounds and are accustomed to using digital technologies in their academic work: both schools are equipped with computer laboratories and digital interactive whiteboards for classroom instruction. As such, the two schools are not fully representative of the broader diversity of school contexts, particularly in terms of socioeconomic background and access to digital resources. 

The experiment was conducted during school hours at the participating schools (Fig. \@ref(fig:classrooms)). About ten experimental sessions were conducted at the schools between November 11 and 12, 2023, in Brussels and February 8 and 9, 2024, in Seville. Each session took about two hours. In the first 45-60 minutes, students received a personal computer and were asked to perform three main tasks using the AI Agent and answer a questionnaire without the AI Agent. In the following 45-60, there was a group discussion on how the students judged the interactions with the AI Agent and a more general debate on how they perceived the potential benefits and drawbacks of integrating LLMs in the classroom. The results of the group discussions are not discussed in this paper; however, they were used as material for interpreting the results of the experimental study.

```{r classrooms, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = cap}
cap <- "Classrooms used for the experiment in Seville (**A**) and in Brussels (**B**)." # nolint
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("assets/pictures/classrooms.pdf"))
```

All participants had appropriate levels of English proficiency, given the language policy of the schools. Even so, the AI Agent was multilingual, allowing students to interact with it either in English or in their native language. The experimental instructions were in English to ensure consistency across sites. However, if needed, students could translate the instructions using the browser's automatic translation service.

## Ethical Approval and Data Privacy

The study received ethical approval from the `r ifelse(params$anonymous, 'Anonymous Institution', 'European Commission')`'s internal Ethical Review Board, ensuring that the consent procedures, data protection requirements, and experimental protocol complied with local laws and ethical research standards.^[Clearance obtained on May 17, 2023.] The data privacy protection protocol was approved by the `r ifelse(params$anonymous, 'Anonymous Institution', 'European Commission')`'s data protection officer. As an additional safeguard, given the minor age of the participants, we required their parents or legal guardians to provide us with written consent, allowing their children to participate in the study. The students also had to give their assent to participate by completing an online consent form.

## Development of the AI Agent

To assess the impact of LLMs on students' performance, we developed an _AI Agent_, a web-based application built using Python with the Flask framework.^[
    In the questionnaires, we used the term "AI tutor" to make it more accessible to the responders.
] The application integrates OpenAI APIs, allowing students to interact with the GPT-4.0 model while performing different educational tasks. This app's key features include:

- **User authentication**: A secure and anonymous login system for students.
- **Web Survey**: A web interface to collect data from students, including answering survey questions and performing simple tasks, such as writing a short essay or solving simple math problems.
- **AI Chatbot**: A chatbot powered by GPT-4 provided students with personalised assistance and tutoring during the session. A new chatbot instance was associated with each question for each student, isolating each conversation from interactions in previous questions. The chatbot was available to students only for specific questions or tasks under the researchers' control.
- **Data logging**: A SQL database storing students' conversation logs with the AI chatbot, including texts, timestamps, and survey responses. 
- **Randomised assignment**: A system to randomly assign registered students to different versions of the AI chatbot or treatment groups to explore the causal impact of various configurations on students' interactions and performance.

## Data

To examine student interactions with AI and their potential impact on learning and performance, we collected a range of self-reported and behavioural data. The full questionnaire is in the Appendix (Section \@ref(questionnaire)).

### AI Attitudes and Usage

To better understand students' general attitudes toward AI, we selected four questions from Schepman and Rodway's AI Attitudes Scale [@schepman2020initial]. These questions explored students' beliefs about AI's societal benefits, potential dangers, capacity to support learning, and the likelihood of misuse by students (Appendix, Section \@ref(questionnaire)). We also asked students about their direct experience using ChatGPT for homework, the most common chatbot at the time of the study, and their beliefs about how many of their peers use ChatGPT for their homework, thereby capturing both individual behaviour and the perceived social norm around AI usage. These measures help establish baseline orientations that may moderate how students engage with and evaluate AI explanations (related to RQ1) and how they perceive different AI interaction guidance (related to RQ3 and RQ4).

### AI Academic Habits and Skills

Academic skills or habits may moderate the effect of AI interactions on problem-solving activities. Accordingly, to account for participants' heterogeneity in academic skills, we asked students to report their average school grades (six-item scale from 5/F to 9/A). We also asked students about their academic habits or the challenges they face at school, such as how often they complete their homework assignments on time (five-item scale from Never to Always) and what factors affect their ability to do so, such as distraction, poor time management or lack of clear instructions from teachers (Appendix, Section \@ref(questionnaire)).

### AI-student Exchanges

For each AI-student conversation (one per task and student) we recorded the number of student messages and the number of words the student wrote. These counts describe how much a student interacted with the agent. They do not measure the quality of the interaction, and they are partly determined by the experimental condition: the Socratic agent was instructed to respond with questions, which invites more replies. We, therefore, do not interpret message counts as engagement, and we adjust for them when comparing the observable content of the conversations (next subsection).

### Coding of the AI-student Exchanges with Large Language Models (LLMs) {#sec:llm-coding}

To address what students and AI agents did in the conversations, beyond how many messages they exchanged, we coded every conversation with LLMs used as raters [@zheng2023judging]. The dialogue was shown to the model with a written rubric, and the model returned an integer score for each item in a fixed format. We coded two sets of items: student behaviour and AI agent response style.

*Student behaviour.* Four items describe what the student wrote: reasoning quality (does the student give reasons or steps of their own), knowledge building (does the student use, extend or test what was said earlier), effort and task focus, and whether the student asked at least one question about the content of the task. The first three were scored 1-5 and the fourth 0/1. Each score level is defined by observable behaviour in the student's own messages (for example, a score of 2 on reasoning means one stated step with no justification). Raters were told to credit only student-authored content, not the pasted task statement, not ideas that only the tutor stated, and not the number of turns. The items are inspired by the ICAP view of learner activity [@chi2014icap], but they measure what is visible in the transcript, not cognition.

*AI agent response style.* We adapted six items from the rubric of Pauzi et al. [@pauzi2025automating] that describe the AI agent's behaviour as Socratic. These are: identifying the student's mistake, acknowledging it, supportive guidance without giving the answer, next-step guidance, conversational flow and encouraging tone, each on a 1-5 scale with behavioural anchors. Four items (supportive guidance, next-step guidance, encouraging tone, conversational flow) are used as a check that the Socratic manipulation worked; the two mistake items apply only when the student made a mistake and were otherwise left empty.

*Raters and procedure.* Each rubric was applied by two LLMs from different providers: OpenAI GPT-4o-mini and Claude Haiku 5.5 for the student items, and Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-4o for the tutor items.^[Exact versions in Appendix \@ref(sec:si-llm-protocol).] Each model rated each conversation once. Student items were rated twice, once with the full dialogue and once with only the student's messages, so that the rater could not see the agent's style.

*Development and holdout.* We wrote and refined the rubrics on a random subset of 40 conversations (20 per condition). During this phase we examined agreement between raters and the difference between conditions, and tightened ambiguous score definitions. The rubrics were then frozen and applied to the remaining 314 conversations (the *holdout* sample). Twelve of these had been rated on a merged Brussels and Seville dialogue, because the conversation identifiers restart in each school, so their ratings are invalid; we dropped them and analyse the remaining 302 conversations (Supporting Information, Section \@ref(sec:si-deviation)), a departure from the pre-specified sample that does not change the rubrics, raters or models. The rating protocol and analysis plan were written after data collection and before the holdout conversations were rated. Primary results use the holdout sample; the 40 development conversations are included only in a sensitivity analysis.

We pre-specified that an item is treated as a primary outcome only if the two raters agree sufficiently on the holdout sample: Krippendorff's alpha (ordinal) of at least 0.67 for 1-5 items [@krippendorff2011alpha], and percent agreement of at least 80% together with Gwet's AC1 of at least 0.60 for the yes/no item [@gwet2008]. Items below these thresholds are reported as exploratory. We did not have human coders.

## Analysis 

### Testing Hypotheses

To guide the empirical analysis, we specified a set of hypotheses corresponding to the five research questions stated in the Introduction (RQ1–RQ5). Each hypothesis maps directly to a specific outcome domain and is tested using the statistical procedures described in the Section \@ref(sec:results).

<!-- RQ1: Does exposure to AI-generated step-by-step reasoning improve students’ problem-solving accuracy? -->

#### H1 (RQ1: Accuracy and Learning Gains)

We hypothesise that exposure to AI-generated explanations improves students’ ability to critically evaluate, update, and refine their initial guesses in the first task (guessing the number of coins in a jar). Specifically, compared to students who receive only the AI-generated estimate, students who receive AI-generated estimate with an explanation are expected to exhibit lower absolute prediction errors and higher post-intervention accuracy.

Furthermore, we hypothesise that providing explanations reduces students’ tendency to blindly reproduce the AI-generated numerical answer without independently adjusting or critically evaluating it.

We test these hypotheses by comparing the distributions of absolute prediction errors across experimental conditions and using non-parametric bootstrap inference to estimate differences in median prediction errors. Additionally, we employ logistic regression to examine whether exposure to AI-generated explanations reduces the probability that students reproduce the AI-generated numerical answer either exactly or within a 10% margin, rather than independently adjusting their predictions.

**H2 (RQ2: Perceived credibility and trust)**.
We hypothesise that providing explicit AI-generated reasoning may reduce perceived reliability of AI outputs by making uncertainty more salient, while also potentially reshaping evaluations of human benchmark performance.  This hypothesis is tested using Fisher’s exact tests and ordinal logistic regression models comparing perceived accuracy ratings across treatments.

**H3a (RQ3: Learning outcomes)**.
We hypothesise that Socratic AI improves learning outcomes relative to non-Socratic tutoring. Learning outcomes are measured only in Task 3 (sound propagation), as the correctness of the answer given after the AI interaction and of the follow-up question answered without AI assistance.

**H3b (RQ3: Confidence)**.
We hypothesise that Socratic AI increases students' self-confidence in their answers.

These hypotheses are tested using regression models with student-level clustering and task fixed effects, as well as ordinal logistic regressions for Likert-scale outcomes.

**H4 (RQ4: Perceived helpfulness)**.
We hypothesise that Socratic AI changes the perceived helpfulness of the AI agent relative to non-Socratic AI. We expected an increase, but students' habits with direct-answer chatbots could push in the opposite direction. This hypothesis is tested with the same models as H3.

**H5a (RQ5: Interaction volume).**
We hypothesise that Socratic AI leads students to send more messages than non-Socratic AI. This is tested with non-parametric comparisons of the number of student messages and words per conversation. Because the Socratic agent was instructed to reply with questions, this difference partly follows from the condition, and we do not treat it as evidence of engagement.

**H5b (RQ5: Observable student reasoning and effort).**
We hypothesise that, in conversations with the Socratic agent, students show more observable reasoning, knowledge building, effort and content questions than students with the non-Socratic agent, over and above the greater number and length of their messages. This is tested with linear mixed models of LLM-coded scores (see \@ref(sec:analysis-llm)).

**H5c (RQ5: Socratic conduct, manipulation check).**
We hypothesise that the Socratic agent scores higher than the non-Socratic agent on supportive guidance, next-step guidance, encouraging tone and conversational flow, as coded by LLM raters. These items capture the pedagogical quality of the AI's responses (scaffolding, stepwise guidance, encouraging tone) and serve as a check that the manipulation worked.

**Exploratory analysis (heterogeneous effects).** We also explore whether the Socratic effects in H3–H5 differ by student characteristics (prior ChatGPT experience, gender, school and task). These analyses add interactions between condition and each covariate to the models above. They were not pre-specified as confirmatory hypotheses, and we report them as exploratory.

### Statistical analysis of the coded dialogues {#sec:analysis-llm}

For each item, each rater's scores were standardised (z-scores over all rated conversations) and the two raters' standardised scores were averaged; the yes/no item was averaged as 0, 0.5 or 1. We estimated linear mixed models of the item score with a random intercept for student, since students contributed one to four conversations, and fixed effects for condition, school and the order of the conversation within the student. 

The primary specification also adjusts for the logarithm of the number of student messages and of the number of student words, because these differ strongly between conditions. We also report the model without this adjustment, which mixes the effect of the agent on what students did with the mechanical effect of the condition on how much they typed. 

Coefficients are reported as differences between the Socratic and non-Socratic conditions in standardised units with 95% confidence intervals. We corrected for multiple testing with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure [@benjamini1995] within each family of four items (student behaviour; AI agent Socratic conduct).

We used non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon rank-sum) for the number of messages and words, which are strongly right-skewed, and linear mixed models for the standardised averages of ordinal ratings. 
<!-- [To reconsider: cumulative-link models on each rater's raw scores are a straightforward robustness check, and ordinal mixed models are an alternative primary analysis.] -->

Sensitivity analyses: (i) ratings made on student messages only; (ii) each rater analysed separately; (iii) excluding conversations in which the student sent a single message; (iv) including the 40 development conversations; and (v) comparing how much of the variation in each score is accounted for by message and word counts alone.
